newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania angry over Italian call for Berisha to quit.
newsitem.headline: Albania angry over Italian call for Berisha to quit.

text.p: A diplomatic row cast doubts over a planned international aid mission to Albania, as Tirana reacted angrily to an Italian official's call for the president of the anarchic Balkan state to quit.

Albania's Foreign Ministry handed a strongly worded protest to Italy's ambassador to Tirana late on Tuesday seeking clarification over deputy Foreign Minister Piero Fassino's call for President Sali Berisha to resign.
The note bluntly asked the ambassador in Tirana to explain Italy's position before Rome made any further decisions regarding Albania.

It was a thinly veiled reference to a vote due on Wednesday in Rome on whether the lower house of parliament will back the centre-left government of Romano Prodi and vote to send troops on a peacekeeping mission to Albania next week.

"Albania's Foreign Ministry asks...for the Italian Foreign Ministry, before the adoption of any other decision, to clarify the position of the Italian government regarding the irresponsible statements of deputy Foreign Minister Fassino," said the note, published by the state-controlled ATA news agency.
Tirana earlier rejected Fassino's remarks as an unacceptable interference into Albania's domestic affairs.
Italy plans to lead the multinational force of some 6,000 troops, who will protect the delivery of emergency food and medicine supplies. They are expected to arrive on April 14.
"The irresponsible statement (by Fassino) only serves to divide and further destabilise the situation in Albania," said Berisha's spokesman in a statement released to journalists.
More than 200 people have been killed and 700 injured in weeks of armed rampage that have swept Albania, Europe's poorest nation, since get-rich-quick investment schemes collapsed earlier this year.
Relations with Italy were already tense following the sinking last month of a boat carrying more than 100 Albanian refugees as it was pursued by an Italian naval vessel. More than 80 people died.
Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi, whose centre-left government has been badly split over Italy's plans to lead the mission to Albania, distanced himself from Fassino's remarks.
He wrote to Berisha and Prime Minister Bashkim Fino assuring them Italy would not meddle in internal Albanian affairs.

Prodi told the Senate earlier that both Italian credibility abroad and the fate of Albanians would be at risk if Italy failed to live up to its task. The multinational force is the first of its kind to be led by Italy.
"It is not rhetoric but the pure and simple truth to say that the whole world is watching us," he said.

Rebel committees holding southern Albanian towns are demanding Berisha's immediate resignation, blaming him for the failure to control popular but fraudulent pyramid savings schemes whose collapse sparked last month's explosion of violence.
He has said he will quit if his Democratic Party loses early elections due to take place by the end of June.
The diplomatic row came as Albania, struggling to restore law and order after weeks of armed anarchy, was increasing security for judges and worked to repair ransacked jails.
Albania's emergency all-party government was trying to restore confidence in its judicial system by assigning special police forces to guard judges.
An armoured personel carrier took up position in front of the Tirana district court as it prepared to reopen after weeks of mayhem.

In a further promising sign that the violence and chaos that erupted over failed investment schemes might be abating, several idle factories in the northern district of Shkoder resumed clothing production and wood processing.
And at a confidence-building military parade shown repeatedly on state-owned television, Defence Minister Shaqir Vukaj said the army needed to look to the future.
"We are not here to talk about what happened," he said. "We are here to restructure the army. We need a new army that serves the country and the people, and not political parties."
